historical_record.description: Voters passed Health and Hospital Bond No. 56 ($3.5 million), whose campaign promised an emergency hospital unit and health center for the Ocean Avenue–Alemany Boulevard district; it paid for the Alemany buildings.
The City bought the site at Alemany Boulevard and Onondaga Avenue for an 'Outer Mission District Health Center', an alternative to the Ocean Avenue site named during the bond campaign.

The Board of Supervisors approved the plan to build the Alemany emergency hospital and health center; it was first drawn as one two-story brick and tile building, with the hospital on the ground floor and the health center above.
Construction of the Alemany buildings was only half finished in May 1932.

The Alemany Emergency Hospital (35 Onondaga, reinforced concrete with a brick and terra-cotta front) and the Alemany Health Center (45 Onondaga, wood-frame stucco) were built as a single city project, completed in 1933; the 1931 plan put the cost at $65,000, later revised upward by more than $17,000.
The Alemany Emergency Hospital opened and was dedicated, after a May opening was postponed while funds to equip it were found; Acting Director of Health Dr. Jacques Gray officiated.

Emergency appropriations passed by the Board of Supervisors kept the new Alemany Emergency Hospital open after the health director had threatened to close it; the Potrero Emergency Hospital closed instead.
During the Second World War the Alemany Emergency Hospital closed briefly for lack of doctors.
The Director of Public Health announced the closing of the city's last emergency hospitals — Park, Harbor and Alemany.

In summer 1978 Excelsior and Outer Mission neighbors organized by COMO (Communities of the Outer Mission Organization) occupied the Alemany Emergency Hospital for over a month and a half in a sit-in against its closure, sleeping there and trying to keep first-aid service going.
San Francisco's free emergency hospital system, including the Alemany Emergency Hospital, was shut down despite the sit-in.
After the emergency hospital closed, a restored city ambulance service ran out of the Alemany Emergency Hospital building, still there in May 1980.
The Alemany buildings were leased to St. Luke's Hospital.
Ownership of the buildings passed from the Department of Public Health to the City's Real Estate Division, and they have stood vacant since.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 272, Alemany Emergency Hospital and Health Center.
